```{r setup}
library(tidyverse)
library(p8105.datasets)
data("ny_noaa")
view(ny_noaa)

install.packages("patchwork")
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
```

## Problem 1: NY NOAA

### Load the data and describe it
`ny_noaa` data contain the daily weather observations from 747 New York weather stations from 1981 through 2010. There are 2,595,176 rows and 7 columns. Each row represents one station-day. The measured variables are `prcp`, `snow`, `snwd`, and `tmax`/`tmin`. Missingness is noticeable, especially for max/min temperatures (44% NA) and snow depth (23% NA). Addition to that, there are 15% of snowfall and 6% of precipitation missing. The missingness limits the comparisons between records from different years.

### Cleaning and check snowfall values
```{r}
noaa_clean =
  ny_noaa %>%
  mutate(
    date = as.Date(date),
    year = year(date),
    month = month(date),
    day = day(date),
    across(c(prcp, snow, snwd, tmax, tmin),
           ~ as.numeric(as.character(.x))),
    prcp = prcp / 10, 
    tmax = tmax / 10, 
    tmin = tmin / 10
  )

noaa_clean %>%
  count(snow, sort = TRUE) %>%
  slice_head(n = 5)
```

I created numeric year, month, and day variables from `date`. The data stores precipitation in tenths of a millimeter and temperatures in tenths of a degree Celsius, so I divided those columns by 10 to get the reasonable units. Snowfall and snow depth are already in millimeters so no change was made. 
0 mm is by far the most common snowfall value. The next most common values include 25, 13, and 51 mm. 0 is common because in most records there is no snowfall.

### two-panel plot for averaged Jan and July max t by station and year
```{r}
station_monthly_tmax =
  noaa_clean %>%
  filter(month %in% c(1, 7)) %>%
  group_by(id, year, month) %>%
  summarise(mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(is.finite(mean_tmax)) %>%
  mutate(month = factor(month, 
                        labels = c("January", "July")))

ggplot(station_monthly_tmax,
       aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, group = interaction(id, month))) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.2, linewidth = 0.25) +
  geom_smooth(aes(group = month), se = FALSE) +
  facet_grid(. ~ month) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Mean daily maximum temperature (°C)",
       title = "Mean January and July max temperature by station")
```
The pplot is divided into two panel, separately represening January and July. In each panel, one line represents the record from one station. The blue line summarize the broad temporal pattern. January plot has much more variation. July temperatures are considerably higher and appear less variable across stations. Some station-year observations appear higher or lower than others (outliers) and may need further check.

### tmax vs tmin and snowfall distribution
```{r}
temperature_plot =
  noaa_clean %>%
  filter(!is.na(tmin), !is.na(tmax)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) +
  geom_bin2d(bins = 50) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Daily records") +
  labs(x = "Minimum temperature (°C)",
       y = "Maximum temperature (°C)",
       title = "Daily minimum and maximum temperature")

snowfall_plot =
  noaa_clean %>%
  filter(!is.na(snow), snow > 0, snow < 100) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(year), y = snow)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.alpha = .3, linewidth = .25) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Snowfall (mm)",
       title = "Daily snowfall between 0 and 100 mm") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1))

temperature_plot + snowfall_plot
  
```


## Problem 2: accelerometer data
### Load, clean, merge, tidy
```{r}
nhanes_covar = read_csv("nhanes_covar.csv", skip = 4) 
nhanes_accel = read.csv("nhanes_accel.csv")

nhanes_merged =
  nhanes_covar %>%
  inner_join(nhanes_accel, by = "SEQN") %>% 
  filter(age >= 21, !is.na(sex),!is.na(age), !is.na(BMI), !is.na(education)) %>% 
  mutate(
    sex = factor(sex, levels = c(1, 2), labels = c("Men", "Women")),
    education = factor(education, levels = c(1, 2, 3), labels = c("Less than high school", "High school equivalent", "More than high school"))) 

nhanes_long = 
  nhanes_merged %>% 
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("min"),
    names_to = "minute",
    names_prefix = "min",
    names_transform = list(minute = as.integer),
    values_to = "MIMS"
  )
```

### Participant counts by sex and education
```{r}
sex_and_education = nhanes_merged %>% 
  count(sex, education, name = "participants") %>% 
  pivot_wider(names_from = sex,
              values_from = participants)
```
In the less-than-high-school category, there are 28 men and 27 women. In the high-school-equivalent category, there are 35 men and 23 women. In the more-than-high-school category, there are 56 men and 59 women.

### Age distribution visualization
```{r}
ggplot(
  nhanes_merged,
  aes(x = sex, y = age, fill = sex)
) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = .7, na.rm = TRUE) +
  facet_wrap(~ education) +
  labs(
    x = "Sex",
    y = "Age (years)",
    title = "Age Distributions by Sex and Education Category"
  )
```
Among participants with less than a high school education, men and women have similar age distributions. The median ages are around 60 and 61 years. In the high-school-equivalent category, women have a higher median age (about 62 years) than men (about 53 years), and the age distributions are relatively wide for both groups. In the more-than-high-school category, both men and women are younger, with respectively median ages around 44 and 41 years.

### Total activity over the day vs age
```{r}
nhanes_daily =
  nhanes_merged %>%
  mutate(
    total_activity = rowSums(
      pick(starts_with("min")),
      na.rm = TRUE
    )
  ) %>% 
  relocate(total_activity, .before = min1)

ggplot(nhanes_daily, aes(x = age, y = total_activity, color = sex)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .5, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_grid(~ education) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Total daily MIMS", color = "Sex",
       title = "Total daily activity by age, sex, and education")
```
Particularly total daily activity is lower among older participants, but the relationship varies by education category and sex. For less than high school group, the decline is steep after a peak at 60 years old. For high school equivalent group, activity generally peaks around ages 35–45 and then declines with age for both sexes. Women appear to have a much higher activity levels than men around ages 30–50. For more than high school group, activity levels are relatively stable at younger and middle ages, followed by a decline before 60 years old for both men and women, and men generally appear to have lower activity levels than women.

### 24 hour mean activity
```{r}
minute_summary =
  nhanes_long %>%
  group_by(education, sex, minute) %>%
  summarise(mean_MIMS = mean(MIMS, na.rm = TRUE),
            n_observed = sum(!is.na(MIMS)), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(minute_summary, aes(x = minute, y = mean_MIMS, color = sex)) +
  geom_line(alpha = .5, linewidth = .2, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE, linewidth = .8) +
  facet_grid(~ education) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1, 360, 720, 1080, 1440),
                     labels = c("12 AM", "6 AM", "12 PM", "6 PM", "12 AM")) +
  labs(x = "Time of day", y = "Mean MIMS per minute", color = "Sex",
       title = "Average 24-hour activity by education and sex")
```
All three education groups have similar daily activity patterns. Activity is relatively low around midnight to 5–6 AM, rises sharply after approximately 6 AM, and peaks around noon. It then generally declines during the evening and drops steeply toward midnight. Also, women generally have higher activity levels than men during the daytime, especially among participants with a high-school-equivalent or more-than-high-school education. In the less-than-high-school category, men's and women's activity curves are more similar and they cross at several times.

## Problem 3: citi Bike
### Import, clean, tidy and describe
```{r}
citi_raw = bind_rows(
  read.csv("./citibike/Jan 2020 Citi.csv") %>% mutate(year = 2020, month = "January"),
  read.csv("./citibike/Jan 2024 Citi.csv") %>% mutate(year = 2024, month = "January"),
  read.csv("./citibike/July 2020 Citi.csv") %>% mutate(year = 2020, month = "July"),
  read.csv("./citibike/July 2024 Citi.csv") %>% mutate(year = 2024, month = "July"))

citi_bike = citi_raw %>% 
  mutate(month = factor(month, levels = c("January", "July")),
         weekdays = factor(weekdays, levels = c("Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday","Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday"), ordered = TRUE)) %>% 
  relocate(year, month, .after = ride_id)
```
The combined data contain 99,485 sampled rides and 9 variables: the seven original columns plus `year` and `month`. The rows represent a 1% sample of rides from January and July of 2020 and 2024, restricted by the assignment to rides shorter than four hours. Each record includes a ride ID, bike type, weekday, ride duration in minutes, start and end station names, and rider type (whether it's `member` or `casual`), along with its sampled month and year. I ordered `weekdays` as an factor from Monday through Sunday. Other variables like bike type, rider type, month, and year are represented categorically or numerically according to the meaning and the usefulness for later plot summaries.

### Ride counts by month, year, and rider type
```{r}
ride_counts = citi_bike %>%
  count(year, month, member_casual, name = "rides") %>% 
  pivot_wider(names_from = member_casual, 
              values_from = rides)
```
The counts by month, year, and rider type are stored in `ride_counts`. Members ride more than casual riders in all eight sampling period. There are more rides in July than in January. And also there are a general increase in number of rides in 2024 compared to 2020.

### 5 most popular starting stations (July24)
```{r}
popular_start = citi_bike %>% 
  filter(year == 2024, month == "July") %>%
  count(start_station_name, name = "rides", sort = TRUE) %>% 
  slice_head(n = 5)
```

### Effects of day of the week, month, and year on median ride duration
```{r}
citi_bike %>%
  group_by(year, month, weekdays) %>%
  summarise(median_duration = median(duration, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = weekdays, y = median_duration, group = month,
             color = month, shape = month)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ year, ncol = 1) +
  labs(x = "Day of the week", y = "Median ride duration (minutes)",
       color = "Month", shape = "Month", linetype = "Month",
       title = "Median Citi Bike ride duration by weekday, month, and year")
```
July rides have longer median duration than January rides for every weekday in both years. Weekend medians are also generally longer than weekday medians, with the largest weekend increases in July. Median duration are shorter in the 2024 samples than in the corresponding 2020 samples.

### Ride duration distributions by month, membership, and bike type in 2024
```{r}
citi_bike %>% 
  filter(year == 2024) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = month, y = duration, fill = month)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = .5, linewidth = 0.3, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_violin(alpha = .2, color = NA, na.rm = TRUE) + 
  facet_grid(member_casual ~ rideable_type,
             labeller = labeller(
               member_casual = c(member = "Citi Bike members",
                                  casual = "Casual riders"),
               rideable_type = c(classic_bike = "Classic bike",
                                 electric_bike = "Electric bike"))) + 
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "Month", y = "Ride duration (log 10 of minutes)",
       title = "2024 ride duration by month, rider type, and bike type")
```
Casual riders generally have longer ride durations than members, and median ride durations tend to be longer in July than in January. The distributions are right-skewed, with most rides lasting relatively short periods and a small number of much longer rides. The combination of violin plots and boxplots compares both the overall distribution shapes and the medians and interquartile ranges.
